tasks.q: Ask the user for six whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of two rows of three and display the grid itself, in the form [[9, 4, 1], [7, 0, 2]].
brief: The first three numbers typed are row 0 and the last three are row 1.
tasks.starter: # Two rows of three, then print the grid

tests.why: Two sets of square brackets inside one. If you got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] you made one flat list instead of a list of lists.
The numbers fill the first row before the second - reading them down the columns would give [[9, 7, 5], [8, 6, 4]].
Build a fresh inner list for each row - reusing the same one leaves both rows pointing at the same three numbers.

tasks.fb: Make an empty row list, append three numbers to it, then append that row to the grid - and start a new row list for the next row.

teach.say: A two-dimensional list is a list whose items are themselves lists. Build each row as its own list, then append that row to the grid.

tasks.q: Ask the user for six names and then a row number, one on each line. Store the names in a grid of three rows of two. Display [number of rows], [how many names in one row] and [that row as a list], on three lines.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, and the row number typed in counts from 0.
Print the row as a list, square brackets and all.
tasks.starter: # Three rows of two names, then report on one row

tests.why: Row 1 is the second row. Printing Ada and Bram means you counted the rows from 1.
len(grid) counts the rows and len(grid[0]) counts the names in one row - here that is 3 and 2, so mixing them up shows at once.
Three rows means 2 is the last row number - adding 1 would run off the end of the grid.
Different names, so a row typed in by hand will fail here. Printing grid[r] gives the brackets and quotes for you.

tasks.fb: A grid is a list of lists, so len(grid) is the number of rows and len(grid[r]) is the number of items in one row.

tasks.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line, then a row number and a column number. Store the numbers in a grid of three rows of three and display [the value stored there] and nothing else.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, and both the row and the column count from 0.
tasks.starter: # Three rows of three, then one value out of it

tests.why: The row comes first and the column second - grid[2][1] would give 3 instead.
Row 0, column 0 is the very first value. Printing 8 means you took grid[1][1], so both numbers were counted from 1.
This is the first test with the two numbers swapped round, so it fails any program that reads the column first.
Three rows of three means the last value is at [2][2] - [3][3] is past the end of the grid.
A different grid, so a value typed in by hand will fail here.

tasks.fb: grid[r] is a whole row and grid[r][c] is one item of that row, so the row always comes first.

teach.say: Two sets of brackets: the first picks a row out of the grid, the second picks an item out of that row.

tasks.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line, then a row number and a column number. Store them in a grid of three rows of three and display [that whole row], then [that whole column] on the next line.
brief: Print a row or a column with single spaces between the values, and no brackets or commas.
Row 0 is filled first, and both numbers count from 0.
tasks.starter: # One row across, one column down

tests.why: A whole row is just grid[r], but a column has to be gathered by taking grid[i][c] from every row in turn.
The row runs across and the column runs down, so they share only the first value. Two identical lines means you printed the row twice.
Row 2 and column 2 are the last of each. Counting from 1 would crash or give the wrong line here.

tasks.fb: A row is one item of the grid; a column is not stored anywhere, so you collect it one row at a time.

tasks.q: Ask the user for six whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of two rows of three and display each row on its own line, with single spaces between the values and no brackets or commas.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, and is printed first too.
tasks.starter: # Two rows in, two tidy lines out

tests.why: Two lines of three. Printing the grid itself would give the brackets and commas the brief rules out.
The rows stay separate even when the values repeat - a single print inside both loops would give six lines instead of two.
Build the whole line first and print it once, or use print(v, end=' ') and then an empty print at the end of each row.

tasks.fb: The outer loop is the rows and the inner loop is the values in one row - the line break belongs to the outer loop.

teach.say: A loop over a grid hands you one row at a time, and a loop inside it walks along that row.

tasks.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of three rows of three and display one line per cell, in the form [row] [column] [value], all of row 0 first.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, rows and columns count from 0, and the three values are separated by single spaces.
tasks.starter: # Visit every cell and say where it is

tests.why: The first line must be 0 0 1. If it says 1 1 1 you started both counts at 1 instead of 0.
With every value the same, only the positions change - this shows plainly that they run 0 to 2 in both directions.
Nine lines in total. Six or three means one of the loops is not running the full three times, or the print is in the wrong loop.

tasks.fb: The outer loop counts rows and the inner loop counts columns, so the inner one finishes once for every single step of the outer one.

tasks.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line, then a row number. Store the numbers in a grid of three rows of four and display [the total of that row] and nothing else.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, and the row number counts from 0.
tasks.starter: # Three rows of four, then the total of one row

tests.why: Total the four values in one row, not the first value of every row - that would give 6 whichever row was asked for.
Row 0 is 2, 5, 3, 1 which comes to 11. An answer of 15 is row 1, which means you counted the rows from 1.
Zeros add nothing but the loop still has to visit them, so 0, 0, 9, 3 comes to 12.
A row of zeros still has a total, and it still has to be printed. Three rows means 2 is the last row number.

tasks.fb: merits[r] is a single row and behaves like any other list, so a running total over it works exactly as it always did.

teach.say: grid[r] is one whole row, and a row is an ordinary list, so you can total it the way you would total any list.

tasks.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of three rows of four. Display [the total of each row], one on each line, then [the total of the whole grid] on the last line.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, and its total is printed first.
tasks.starter: # A total for each row, then one for everything

tests.why: Three row totals and then the grand total, so four lines in all - forgetting the last line loses a mark even if the rows are right.
A row of zeros still prints its total of 0 - it must not be skipped.
If every row total is the same as the grand total you forgot to reset the row total back to 0 at the start of each row.

tasks.fb: Set the row total to 0 inside the outer loop, and keep a separate grand total outside it that never gets reset.

tasks.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line, then a column number. Store the numbers in a grid of four rows of three and display [the total of that column] and nothing else.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, and the column number counts from 0.
tasks.starter: # Four rows of three, then the total of one column

tests.why: Gather the column with grid[r][c] from every row - the column number stays the same while the row number changes.
Column 0 is 3, 5, 0, 9 which comes to 17. An answer of 12 means you totalled row 0 instead.
Three columns means 2 is the last one - counting from 1 would ask for column 3 and crash.
Every value in column 1 is 0, so the total is 0. A 4 here means you totalled column 0 whatever was asked for.

tasks.fb: Loop over the rows with range(len(grid)) and hold the column number still - that is the one difference from totalling a row.

teach.say: A column is not stored anywhere, so you gather it one row at a time: the column number stays still while the row number changes.

tasks.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of four rows of three. Display [the total of each column], one on each line, then [the total of the whole grid] on the last line.
brief: Row 0 is filled first, and the total of column 0 is printed first.
tasks.starter: # A total for each column, then one for everything

tests.why: Three column totals then the grand total. Getting 6, 15, 24, 33 means you totalled the rows instead of the columns.
Only column 0 has anything in it - the other two still print a total of 0 rather than being skipped.
Here it is the last column that holds everything, so a loop that stops one column short would print 0, 0 and then the wrong grand total.

tasks.fb: For column totals the outer loop counts columns and the inner loop counts rows - the opposite way round to row totals.

tasks.q: Ask the user for nine names, one on each line, then a name to look for. Display not seated when it is not in the grid, or [row] [column] and then [how many seats in that row are not empty] on the next line.
brief: The nine names fill a grid of three rows of three, row 0 first, and a free seat is typed as the word empty.
Rows and columns count from 0, with a single space between them.
tasks.starter: # Search the grid for the name, then count that row

tests.why: Row first, then column. Printing 2 1 means the two were the wrong way round.
Nia is in the top left, which is row 0 column 0. Printing 1 1 means you counted rows and columns from 1.
Yves is the very last seat, so a search that stops before the end of the last row never finds it. Nobody in row 2 is empty, so the count is 3.
Row 0 has one empty seat, so only two of its three seats count - the word empty must be skipped, not counted.
A name that is nowhere in the grid prints that one line and nothing else, so the row and column must only be printed once the name has been found.

tasks.fb: Two loops to search every cell, a remembered row and column that start at something impossible like -1, then a separate loop over the found row to count the seats.

teach.say: Two loops over range(len(...)) visit every cell of a grid in turn, row by row.

tasks.q: The grid is [[4, 7, 2], [5, 1, 9]]. What does each piece of Python give back?
tasks.fb: The row index always comes first, and both indexes count from 0.

info.title: Rows first
info.text: A grid is described as rows by columns, so a 3 by 4 grid has 3 rows of 4 items each.

info.title: Two notations
info.text: Pseudocode in the exam writes a cell as array[1,2]. Python writes the same cell as grid[1][2].

info.title: One long line
info.text: Memory is one long line of addresses, so a grid is stored row after row. Reading along a row is the natural direction.

info.title: sum() a row
info.text: sum() totals a list, so sum(grid[0]) totals a whole row in one step - but a column still needs a loop.

info.title: Ragged grids
info.text: Nothing stops the rows being different lengths, though most tasks assume they match. Use len(grid[r]) if they might not.

info.title: Three dimensions
info.text: A list of grids is a three-dimensional array, which is how a program might hold a seating plan for every week of term.
